ideas.title: Phantom API
ideas.summary: A party game where you list real functions from a library (Python stdlib, NumPy, the DOM) until you invent one by mistake, then compete against an LLM that is trying not to hallucinate either.
ideas.description: Inspired by 'List Animals Until Failure' from the HN Arcade roundup, this flips the format onto programming APIs, where fabricated names are a real and costly problem (LLM-invented packages and methods are now a known supply-chain risk). Pick a module such as `itertools`, `str`, `Array.prototype` or `pandas.DataFrame`, then type member names one at a time under a shrinking timer. Every answer is checked against a bundled, version-pinned symbol index generated by introspection, so verification is instant and offline. Typing a plausible-but-fake name ends the round and shows the closest real names by edit distance. A 'versus the model' mode asks Claude for the next name in the same list and scores both of you, which makes a surprisingly clear demo of how often confident-sounding APIs are made up.
keyFeatures: Version-pinned symbol indexes built by a script that walks `dir()` / `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` for each supported module
Instant offline validation with 'did you mean' suggestions ranked by Levenshtein distance
Rarity scoring: obscure-but-real names (e.g. `itertools.pairwise`) earn more points than `append`
Versus-the-model mode that logs every hallucinated name the LLM produces, with a running fabrication rate
Shareable result card listing your streak and the one name that sank you
ideas.techStack: React + Vite, Tailwind, Python/Node build script for symbol indexes, Claude API (optional versus mode), Netlify
ideas.whyInteresting: A 1-2 day build with a genuinely viral loop, and it doubles as a five-minute classroom warm-up on API recall and on why you verify AI-suggested function names before trusting them.
ideas.inspiredBy: HN Arcade newsletter issue #1, 'List Animals Until Failure' (https://buttondown.com/andrewgy8/archive/issue-1/)

ideas.title: Peer Pick Ledger
ideas.summary: Mines a course forum export to find which videos, docs and tutorials students actually recommend to each other, ranked by endorsement and sentiment, so instructors can see the shadow curriculum.
ideas.description: Inspired by an r/SideProject post that analyzed 14 million Reddit comments to rank what products people genuinely recommend, this applies the same idea to a course discussion board. The instructor uploads an Ed Discussion or Piazza export; the tool extracts every external link and named resource (YouTube videos, Stack Overflow answers, blog posts, other universities' notes), resolves duplicates, and classifies the surrounding sentence as a recommendation, a complaint, or a neutral mention. The result is a weekly leaderboard of peer-endorsed resources tied to the assignment or topic thread they appeared in. Instructors can promote a resource into the official course page, flag one that teaches an outdated or incorrect approach, or notice that half the class learned recursion from the same video.
keyFeatures: Importers for Ed Discussion JSON and Piazza CSV exports, with student names stripped on ingest
URL canonicalization and title fetching to merge duplicate links (youtu.be vs youtube.com, tracking params)
Mention classification (recommend / complain / neutral) using a small local model or the `claude` CLI in batch
Per-topic and per-week leaderboards with a timeline of when each resource caught on
One-click 'promote to course resources' and 'flag as misleading' actions that generate a forum announcement draft
ideas.techStack: Flask, SQLite, React + Vite, Tailwind, local sentiment model or `claude` CLI batch jobs
ideas.whyInteresting: Every course has a hidden reading list made of whatever students share with each other; surfacing it tells instructors what explanations are actually landing, and it is a realistic data-pipeline project with privacy constraints.
ideas.inspiredBy: r/SideProject post on dharm.is, ranking products from 14M Reddit comments with a fine-tuned RoBERTa sentiment model (via gummysearch.com/r/SideProject/)

ideas.title: Build Your Own Micropolis
ideas.summary: A staged assignment where students build a SimCity-style city simulator from scratch: zoning grid, power-network flood fill, traffic pathfinding, diffusion-based land value and pollution, and a growth model that ties them together.
ideas.description: Inspired by a Show HN post of a SimCity clone written entirely in Emacs Lisp, this assignment uses the city builder as a vehicle for a semester's worth of core algorithms. Phase 1 is a tile grid with zoning and a render loop. Phase 2 adds the power grid as connected-component labeling (BFS flood fill from power plants). Phase 3 adds traffic: each zone sends trips to the nearest job or shop tile using Dijkstra on the road graph, with congestion feeding back into edge costs. Phase 4 adds pollution, crime and land value as diffusion over the grid (repeated blur kernels), and Phase 5 adds the growth rule that lets zones develop or decay based on those fields. Each phase ships with deterministic seed maps and expected snapshots, so autograding compares field values rather than screenshots.
keyFeatures: Five phased milestones, each mapping to one algorithmic idea (grid modeling, flood fill, shortest paths, diffusion, cellular rules)
Deterministic seeded maps with golden JSON snapshots for autograding each subsystem independently
Debug overlays students must implement: power coverage, traffic heatmap, land value field
Performance target (a 128x128 city ticking at 30 Hz) that motivates incremental updates over full recomputation
Optional stretch: budget and tax model, or a 'mayor agent' that places zones to maximize population
ideas.techStack: TypeScript + Canvas (or Python + pygame), Vitest or pytest snapshot tests, GitHub Classroom
ideas.whyInteresting: Students get a playable, show-off-able game while practicing BFS, Dijkstra, convolution and simulation design in one coherent codebase, and the feedback loops between subsystems teach systems thinking that isolated exercises cannot.
ideas.inspiredBy: elcity, a Micropolis/SimCity clone in Emacs Lisp featured in HN Arcade issue #1 (https://github.com/vkazanov/elcity)

ideas.title: Round-Trip Narration Fidelity: A Reconstruction Benchmark for Screen-Reader Descriptions of Program State
ideas.summary: Builds an automatic benchmark that scores nonvisual descriptions of stack-and-heap program state by whether the structure (including aliasing, sharing and cycles) can be reconstructed from the narration alone, so accessible program visualizers can be evaluated before user studies.
ideas.description: The 'Born Accessible' Scheme visualizer work designs navigable, narrated views of lists, pairs, vectors and structs for blind and low-vision learners, but evaluating such narrations currently requires scarce BLV participants. This project proposes a round-trip test: generate program states from a corpus of CS1/CS2 programs, render each through a narration strategy (linear screen-reader text, hierarchical ARIA tree, LLM-written summary, Python Tutor-style alt text), then have an independent reconstructor (rule-based parser and LLM) rebuild the box-and-pointer graph from the narration only. Fidelity is graph-isomorphism accuracy plus targeted probes on the features that most often break mental models, such as shared substructure, aliasing after mutation, and cyclic references. The result is a reusable benchmark and a ranked set of narration design rules that tool builders can apply before running a smaller, better-targeted human study.

papers.title: "Born Accessible" Visualizers for Scheme Program State
papers.authors: Jacob Bell, Salyan Karki, William Pitchford, Anna Deschamps, Eva Kapoor, Elene Sturua, Charles Wade, et al. (Grinnell College)
papers.abstract: Tools such as Python Tutor show the value of giving students a visual model of program state, but many of these visualizations are inaccessible to blind and low-vision learners. The authors describe the design and implementation of an accessible visualizer for Scheme program state in the Scamper pedagogical IDE, covering lists, pairs, vectors and structs, with navigation support for substructures and approaches to narrating each component.
papers.relevance: Supplies the design space (navigation plus narration of structured runtime state) that this project turns into a measurable benchmark; its narration strategies become the first systems evaluated.

additionalRefs.title: Nonvisual Support for Understanding and Reasoning about Data Structures (Arboretum)
additionalRefs.authors: Brianna L. Wimer, Ritesh Kanchi, Kaija Frierson, Venkatesh Potluri, Ronald Metoyer, Jennifer Mankoff, Miya Natsuhara, Matt X. Wang
additionalRefs.relevance: Compiles data-structure diagram specs into tabular, navigable and tactile formats and finds that format choice matters by task; provides comparison formats and task types for the benchmark's probes.

additionalRefs.title: Olli: An Extensible Visualization Library for Screen Reader Accessibility
additionalRefs.authors: Matt Blanco, Jonathan Zong, Arvind Satyanarayan
additionalRefs.relevance: Establishes hierarchical, multi-granularity ARIA tree views as a principled way to narrate structured visuals; one of the narration strategies to adapt from charts to heap graphs.

additionalRefs.title: Accessible AST-Based Programming for Visually-Impaired Programmers
additionalRefs.authors: Emmanuel Schanzer, Sina Bahram, Shriram Krishnamurthi
additionalRefs.relevance: Shows structure-aware navigation improves orientation and accuracy for blind programmers on code trees; motivates extending structural navigation from source code to runtime state.

additionalRefs.title: Online Python Tutor: Embeddable Web-Based Program Visualization for CS Education
additionalRefs.relevance: The de facto visual stack-and-heap notional machine; its execution-trace JSON format provides a ready source of ground-truth program states for the benchmark.

researchPlan.overview: First build a corpus of ground-truth program states with known structural traps, then implement several narration strategies and an automatic reconstructor that scores them by round-trip fidelity. Finally, analyze which narration features predict fidelity, release the benchmark, and use the results to design a small, targeted follow-up study with BLV learners.

milestones.goal: Literature review on nonvisual program and data-structure representations; define the state graph schema and fidelity metrics
milestones.deliverable: Annotated bibliography, state-graph JSON schema, metric definitions (isomorphism accuracy, alias/cycle probe accuracy)

milestones.goal: Generate ground-truth states by tracing CS1/CS2 programs (Python via Python Tutor backend, Scheme via Scamper) and add synthetic states with aliasing, sharing and cycles
milestones.deliverable: Corpus of 2,000+ labeled program states stratified by structural feature

milestones.goal: Implement narration strategies: linear screen-reader text, hierarchical ARIA tree serialization, Born-Accessible-style component narration, and LLM-written summaries
milestones.deliverable: Narration library with four or more strategies and rendered outputs for the full corpus

milestones.goal: Build reconstructors (deterministic parser where possible, plus open and hosted LLMs) and score every strategy
milestones.deliverable: Fidelity leaderboard with per-feature breakdowns and failure examples

milestones.goal: Ablate narration design choices (naming of shared nodes, depth limits, back-reference phrasing, verbosity) and derive design rules
milestones.deliverable: Ranked narration design guidelines with effect sizes; draft of BLV follow-up study protocol
Submitted paper plus open-source benchmark and narration library

researchPlan.resources: Python Tutor backend and Scamper for tracing; a corpus of CS1/CS2 exercises (open sets such as CodeWorkout or course archives); modest LLM budget via the local `claude` CLI or an open model (Llama/Qwen) for reconstruction; one undergraduate research assistant for corpus curation; contact with a BLV accessibility consultant for face validity review.

risks.risk: Round-trip reconstructability may not match what BLV learners actually find usable (a narration can be complete but cognitively overwhelming)
risks.mitigation: Report verbosity and navigation cost alongside fidelity, frame results as a necessary-condition filter, and validate top and bottom strategies in a small follow-up study with BLV learners

risks.risk: LLM reconstructors may infer structure from priors rather than the narration, inflating scores
risks.mitigation: Include adversarial states that violate typical patterns, use a deterministic parser baseline, and test with shuffled or ablated narrations as controls

risks.risk: Scheme-specific structures may not generalize to Python or Java object graphs
risks.mitigation: Build the corpus language-neutral from the start (state-graph schema) and include Python traces alongside Scheme
